scenes.visual: Title card: Similar Bodies, Different Branches.

scenes.tts: A nematode and an earthworm look a lot alike. Both are long, soft worms, with a gut that runs from mouth to anus. Yet gene comparisons put them on different branches of the animal tree. The nematode groups with insects, and other animals that moult. The earthworm groups with snails and flatworms. Body-plan characters are how we describe an animal. On their own, they do not tell us who is related to whom.

scenes.tts: Libbie Hyman's great survey of the invertebrates sorted these animals by body cavity. Acoelomates, like a planarian flatworm, have tissue between gut and body wall. Pseudocoelomates, like a nematode, have a cavity without a full mesoderm lining. Coelomates, like the earthworm, have a cavity lined entirely by mesoderm. A group like this is a grade, a shared level of organization. A clade is different. It is an ancestor and all of its descendants.

scenes.visual: Three bins by body cavity with planarian, nematode and earthworm cross-sections; label grade; then a branching bracket labelled clade.

scenes.tts: In 1997, Aguinaldo, Lake and colleagues compared the eighteen S ribosomal R N A gene across animals. Nematodes grouped with arthropods and other moulting animals, not with annelids. Both moult a cuticle, so the group is called Eck-dih-so-ZO-uh. Later analyses of many genes broadly support it. They put flatworms inside Spiralia, with annelids and molluscs, among relatives that have a coelom. So body cavity describes a grade, not a clade.
scenes.visual: The bins are rebuilt into a tree: nematode joins arthropod in Ecdysozoa; flatworm, annelid and mollusc chips form Spiralia; the cavity labels stay attached and now scatter across branches.

scenes.tts: These characters are still the right way to describe an animal. Symmetry: none, as in a sponge, or radial, or bilateral. Germ layers: two, or three, with a middle layer called mesoderm. A body cavity, or none. And keep the gut apart from the cavity: even a planarian has a gut.

scenes.tts: These characters shape how an animal lives. A through gut moves food one way, so each region can do its own job, from a grinding gizzard to a long intestine. A sealed, fluid-filled segment works as a hydrostatic skeleton. Squeeze it narrower, and at constant volume it gets longer. Waves of this push an earthworm through the soil.

scenes.tts: Old developmental rules need the same test. In a slipper snail, traced cells showed that the blastopore becomes the mouth, as the old mouth-first rule predicts. But blastopore fate varies, even among close relatives, so it is not a reliable test of the major clades. To test a grouping, sample many genes, and add independent evidence, such as which genes share chromosomes. Body-plan characters describe animals. Independent evidence tests their ancestry.
scenes.visual: Small snail embryo chip, blastopore to mouth; a caution chip; evidence chips (many genes, shared chromosomes) converge on the tree; final rule on screen.
